Best European Cities To Visit With Kids

By Marcus Webb · March 5, 2026 · Updated August 10, 2026

The idea that European city trips don’t work with young kids usually comes from trying to do a European city trip the way you would without them — long museum days, dinner reservations at 9pm, and a walking pace built for adults. Done differently, several European cities are genuinely excellent family destinations.

This list sticks to cities that hold up well at a family’s pace, with specific sights and neighborhoods that make the difference rather than a generic “here’s what to see” rundown.

What makes a European city work for a family trip

Not every European city is an easy family trip. The ones that work well tend to share a few things: compact old centers you can cross on foot, parks scattered through the city rather than on the outskirts, and enough hands-on museums to break up the churches-and-galleries pace that trips adults.

We've focused this list on cities where a family can build a genuinely enjoyable four or five days without feeling like every stop is a compromise for the kids.

Top picks

Copenhagen

Consistently the easiest European city with young kids — Tivoli Gardens is a real theme park in the city center, cycling infrastructure is excellent, and playgrounds are everywhere.

Amsterdam

Flat, canal-lined, and easy to navigate with a stroller or bikes. NEMO Science Museum is one of the better hands-on museums in Europe for kids 6 and up.

Paris

Works better than its reputation suggests if you plan around kid-paced sights — a Seine boat ride, the Jardin du Luxembourg's playgrounds, and the top of the Arc de Triomphe instead of a full Louvre day.

Lisbon

Hillier than the others on this list, but the trams double as an attraction, the food is forgiving of picky eaters, and it's one of the better value options in Western Europe.

Things kids tend to enjoy

  • Tivoli Gardens, Copenhagen — an actual amusement park inside the city
  • A hop-on boat tour on the Seine or Amsterdam's canals — sightseeing without the walking
  • NEMO Science Museum, Amsterdam
  • Lisbon's Tram 28 route, which covers most major sights as a ride rather than a walk

Travel tips

  • Plan one real 'kid choice' activity per day alongside anything adults want to see — it resets the mood faster than pushing through
  • Book skip-the-line tickets for major sights in summer; European city queues in July and August are long
  • Cobblestones are hard on strollers — a lightweight umbrella stroller often works better than a full travel system
  • Many European museums are free or discounted for kids under a certain age (varies by country, often 12 or 18) — check before buying

Frequently asked questions

What is the easiest European city to visit with young kids?

Copenhagen is the most consistently recommended — it's flat, has excellent playgrounds and parks, and Tivoli Gardens is a genuine theme park in the middle of the city.

Is Paris a good city for a family trip with young kids?

Yes, if you plan around their pace rather than a typical adult itinerary — shorter museum visits, more park and boat-ride time, and realistic expectations about how much of the Louvre a six-year-old will tolerate.

How many days do you need in a European city with kids?

Four to five days is usually enough to see the highlights at a family pace without feeling rushed, and leaves room for at least one slow, unplanned day.
